item.title: Gold trims gains after overnight strikes on Iran as the focus turns to the US midterm elections
item.description:
Gold spiked to the upside yesterday as expectations for a US-Iran deal strengthened after Iran’s President said that the Supreme Leader granted the government certain authorities regarding negotiations.

The markets took the news as a signal for greater flexibility to reach a deal since strategic decisions remain under the authority of the Supreme Leader.

The gains faded, though, after the US struck sites on Iran’s Qeshm Island overnight, with US officials saying the strike was in response to Iran firing at a US aircraft and did not mark the start of expanded US operations.

Trump said that he’s not looking to strike Iran after the midterm elections, but officials confirmed that he’s weighing all options. Moreover, Axios reported that the CIA Director advised Trump to maintain a “no war, no deal” approach and let economic pressure on Iran continue.

Looking ahead, today we have the US midterm elections, although we will get the first results very late in the day. The Democrats are widely expected to take the House, so that should be already priced in. The more out of consensus outcomes would be a red sweep and a blue sweep.

In the first case, we could see gold coming under pressure amid further tax cuts and higher defence spending potentially leading to a repricing in Treasury yields to the upside. In the second scenario, we could see the opposite of that as a Democratic victory would likely bring legislative gridlock on the agenda.

If we get another retest of the support and the major upward trendline, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the trendline, to position for a rally into new record highs. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

item.title: Swiss inflation surprises higher in October but core prices offer some relief
item.description:
• Switzerland October CPI +1.5% vs +1.3% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.0%
  • Switzerland October core CPI +0.5% y/y
  • Prior +0.5%

Swiss headline annual inflation picks up at the start of the third quarter, rising to 1.5% from 1.0% previously. Much like elsewhere around the region, higher energy prices are the main culprit in continuing to feed through to consumer prices. As such, the inflation numbers may look to be heating up again at first glance.

But in looking to core annual inflation, that remains unchanged at just 0.5%. That tells us that the broader inflation picture isn't quite as alarming as the headline reading might suggest.

And for the SNB, that is the most crucial takeaway here. The central bank has been arguing for months that higher energy costs are largely responsible for the inflation pickup, with limited evidence of second-round effects spilling over to the wider economy.

The latest figures we're seeing today doesn't really challenge that narrative as such.

Naturally, headline inflation moving closer to the 2% mark does mean that policymakers won't be entirely comfortable if energy prices continue to stay elevated. That will especially be the case if there is more evidence of businesses eventually passing those higher costs on to consumers.

But at least for now, the SNB still has room to sit comfortably on the sidelines and assess how persistent these inflation pressures might become. In other words, there's no reason to panic just yet.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US-Iran deal still out of reach despite fresh diplomatic hopes ahead of US midterms
item.description:
And round and round we go. We started the week with renewed optimism that the US and Iran might finally be inching towards a diplomatic breakthrough. That led to oil prices tumbling on Monday as hopes of a potential deal gathered momentum. But fast forward to today, and we're pretty much back where we started.

Anyone got a case of déjà vu? These have been the same sort of headlines that we have been dealing with for almost seven months now.

The latest comments from a senior Iranian official to Reuters:

  • Tehran's conditions must be met if the US wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, with nuclear talks only possible afterwards
  • Iran is prepared to respond forcefully to US strikes, both in the region and beyond
  • Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington

Now, that is hardly the language of two sides getting ready to shake hands.

The thing about all this is that the sticking point remains the same. Iran wants its demands addressed before reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while the US is not willing to agree to those terms. And despite the diplomatic exchanges, neither side appears ready to make the concessions needed to break the deadlock.

For markets, it just exemplifies the narrative that the underlying geopolitical risks haven't gone anywhere.

While Monday's selloff in the oil market may have shown how quickly traders were willing to price in a potential easing of tensions, the fact of the matter is the reality is not quite there yet.

There's been a lot of talk about what could happen once the US midterms are over and done with. So, we'll have to see if Trump will be bold enough to step up his game after the election later today. The real test will come after the votes are cast, when we'll see whether diplomacy can produce anything concrete or whether the threat of renewed military escalation returns to the forefront. Knowing Trump as we do, the latter certainly seems rather likely.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA governor Bullock says it might be that this rate hike might not be enough
item.description:
In case you missed it, the RBA raised its cash rate by 25 bps to 4.85% today in a less straightforward 6-3 vote. That takes the cash rate to the highest level in 18 years, with the central bank trying not to pre-commit to further tightening at this stage. So far, Bullock's tone in her press conference has been more neutral and even in the latest remarks here.

She says that the rate hike today might not be the last one but in trying to make that judgment, "it is not as obvious" as compared to before. Adding that she doesn't know how high rates will need to go and that it is up to the market to interpret their messaging.

Bullock continues to reaffirm that the central bank will stay on a data-dependent path in saying that "it is probably good to wait now and assess incoming data".

Having said that, she continues to at least highlight that inflation remains a key concern heading into next year. But at least for now, the dissenting votes should tone down any overly hawkish expectations from the central bank for the immediate outlook.

As mentioned here, markets were not pricing in strong odds of another rate hike to follow up the one today. And so, the RBA is reaffirming those expectations for the most part with their choice of language and communique this week.

AUD/USD is down 0.3% on the day to 0.6975 currently, with the technicals also emphasising a rejection at the 100 and 200-day moving averages amid a fall back below 0.7000 today:

The drop now puts into focus the swing region support around 0.6900-15 next with the trendline support from the April to June lows also holding thereabouts. So, that will be the first immediate downside risk level before the June lows come into play around 0.6865-75 next.

As for buyers, the onus is on them to try and arrest the decline to get back above 0.7000 first. But even then, there will be stubborn resistance from the 100-day (red line) and 200-day (blue line) moving averages around 0.7030-56 to get through.

With the RBA now out of the way, the focus for AUD/USD now turns to the US midterm elections instead. That will potentially be the next key trigger for a notable move in the dollar, with traders watching how Republicans are going to fare in defending both chambers in Congress from falling to Democratic control.

item.title: Apple earnings beat fails to impress Wall Street as tech shares struggle ahead of US midterms
item.description:
Another week and it's another big tech name that is finding out that even beating earnings estimates isn't good enough for Wall Street these days. Apple is that next big name to be struck down and the timing couldn't be worse for an already battered tech sector in markets.

Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $114.48 billion and earnings per share of $2.10, beating expectations of $113.39 billion and $1.99 respectively. Now, that sounds pretty decent no?

Well, if only the market reaction shared that view. Apple shares instead are down 2% in after-hours trading as investors turned their attention to the less flattering details.

As always, it is all about the guidance. Of note, Apple expects gross margins to decline to around 45-46% for the December quarter, down from 47.9%, as rising memory costs squeeze profitability. Meanwhile, services revenue growth is also projected at just 8-9% and that comes under expectations of around 10.7%.

Besides that, there is also the fact that tariff refunds have flattered the latest quarterly results. So, there is good reason to question how much of the latest earnings strength will carry forward to the next one.

In any case, we have seen over the past few weeks how Wall Street is turning more and more unforgiving when it comes to techn earnings especially. It's not enough to deliver good numbers anymore and disappointing outlooks are being punished hard. And that's not the sort of backdrop that encourages investors to rush back into expensive tech names.

The S&P 500 fell by 0.5% yesterday with the Nasdaq falling by another 1.1%. However, I feel what really jumps out of the page with the market showing yesterday is the fact that stocks were off to a good start initially. The S&P 500 surrendered 1.1% gains to close lower as the heavy selling pressure remains concentrated in tech rather than spreading evenly across the market. For some context, the Dow closed up by 0.4%.

If anything, it reaffirms that concerns surrounding AI spending, valuations and future profitability aren't going away just yet.

And today, we have the US midterm elections to add to the mix. As such, Wall Street has another reason to be careful.

The battle for control of Congress will be the main event, with investors watching whether Republicans can retain both chambers or whether Democrats can make gains that could complicate the Trump administration's fiscal and legislative agenda.

  • US midterms 2026: Is Trump about to lose his grip on Congress?
  • US midterms 2026: Where are Republicans most vulnerable in the battle for Congress?

Looking to the day ahead, I'll be watching whether Apple drags the broader tech sector lower and whether we see another early rebound fade before the closing bell.

The midterms might provide a distraction or perhaps even some relief if political uncertainty clears later in the day. But for tech shares, the pain seems to be running deeper and things might actually get worse before they get any better.

item.title: RBA’s Bullock offers no guidance, says it is probably good to wait for data after hike
item.description:
Earlier:

Bullock’s comments sent a mixed signal for the Australian dollar and the front end of the curve. Her warning that inflation is largely locked in for the next year, and that unemployment must rise further, underlines the RBA’s resolve. Her account of the dissent, though, suggests a significant minority is already wary of overtightening. That balance supports the view that further hikes remain possible but are far from assured, limiting the scope for a strong rebound in the AUD after its post-decision dip. For Australian equities, the explicit acceptance of weaker growth and higher unemployment adds to pressure on rate-sensitive sectors such as banks, retailers and property, which the RBA itself identified as under strain. 

Bullock’s suggestion that the board should now wait for data tilts the balance toward a pause, reducing the chance of a near-term follow-up hike and capping the AUD’s rebound potential.

--

Bullock made the case for accepting some economic pain now to stop inflation becoming entrenched, but her description of the dissent shows a board increasingly divided over how far to push. 

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Michele Bullock said the rate rise was needed to bring inflation down and was aimed at addressing local capacity pressures
  • She said growth will need to remain subdued and unemployment will need to rise further
  • Bullock argued that accepting some pain now would prevent greater pain later
  • The three members who voted to hold saw more downside risks and felt the board should wait longer for data
  • Bullock said inflation is largely baked in for the next year, describing that as not a good situation to be in
  • The RBA raised its cash rate 25 basis points to 4.85% earlier on Tuesday in a 6-3 vote, its highest level in 18 years
  • Bullock said she does not know what the next rate move will be, offered no guidance and said it is probably good to wait now and see incoming data.
  • Bullock said monetary policy will work but takes time to feed through, noting unemployment is still relatively low, jobs growth continues and she does not see the economy cracking

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said on Tuesday that the central bank’s latest rate rise was needed to bring inflation down, and that the economy will have to endure subdued growth and higher unemployment to get there.

Speaking at her press conference after the board lifted the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85%, Bullock said the tightening was aimed at domestic capacity pressures. She argued that accepting some pain now would help prevent further pain down the track. Growth will need to stay subdued and unemployment to rise further, she said.

Bullock was frank about the near-term inflation outlook. She said inflation is largely baked in for the next year and described that as not a good situation to be in. The comments align with the RBA’s updated forecasts, released alongside the decision, which see headline inflation peaking at 4.5% in the December quarter and both headline and trimmed mean inflation staying above 3% until late 2027.

The governor also shed light on the board’s division. Six members voted for the hike and three preferred to hold at 4.60%. Bullock said those favouring a hold saw greater downside risks to the economy and felt the board should wait a little longer for more data before acting. 

On the outlook, Bullock said she does not know what the next move in rates will be and that the board is not offering forward guidance. She added that it would probably be sensible to wait now and assess incoming data, comments likely to reinforce speculation that Tuesday’s increase could be followed by a pause.

The RBA publishes its votes without attributing them to individual members, so the identities of the dissenters have not been disclosed.

The hike, the RBA’s fifth this year, takes the cash rate to its highest level since 2008. In its statement, the board said it would remain attentive to the data and do what is necessary to return inflation to target, without explicitly committing to further increases. The Australian dollar fell after the decision, which markets had widely expected, amid some speculation that the split vote could mean this is the last hike of the cycle. 

Bullock also expressed confidence that the tightening will have the intended effect, saying monetary policy works but takes time to feed through to the economy. She noted that unemployment remains relatively low and that jobs growth is continuing, adding that she does not see the economy cracking at this point.

---

Oil and Iran

Crude ticked up after falling about 4% on Monday, when mediated talks between Iran and the US raised hopes of a deal. US aircraft struck Iranian sites on Qeshm Island, at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz, after Iran shot down a US MQ-9 Reaper drone, according to reports. China and the yuan

The People’s Bank of China said it would raise the foreign exchange deposit reserve ratio for financial institutions to 6% from 4%, effective November 15, a move that reduces onshore dollar liquidity. It also set its daily reference rate with the dollar higher. Together, the steps point to a desire to slow the yuan’s recent appreciation, and could herald a period of consolidation for the currency. With Chinese interest rates low relative to peers, that could also add to the offshore yuan’s appeal as a funding currency.

The offshore yuan fell 0.26% to 6.6642 per dollar, its largest daily decline since June.

Most Asian markets followed US technology shares lower. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.7% and the Kosdaq dropped 3.8%, extending recent pressure on the region’s chip-heavy markets. Earnings and AI financing

On the call, it guided to 7% to 10% revenue growth in the December quarter but a gross margin of 45% to 46%, below the prior quarter’s guided range, as memory prices keep rising and Siri AI costs weigh. item.title: Apple and Palantir beat earnings. Why did both stocks fall?
item.description:
Apple and Palantir beat earnings. Wall Street is still hard to impress

Apple's profit-margin outlook and Palantir's demanding growth expectations have left investors cautious despite strong reported numbers. Our simplified Earnings Mood Score stands at 4/10, highlighting why the market's reaction matters as much as the earnings themselves.

Apple (AAPL) and Palantir (PLTR) delivered stronger-than-expected quarterly results on November 2, yet both stocks moved lower after hours. Neither decline exceeded the options market's expected move, but the reactions reinforce a broader message from this earnings season: investors remain selective, and impressive numbers alone are not always enough.

That doesn't mean Wall Street is in panic mode. It does suggest investors are becoming harder to impress, particularly when large companies or popular growth stocks face elevated expectations.

Apple and Palantir: Strong earnings, weaker stock reactions

Apple (AAPL): -2.81% after hours

Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year over year, and earnings per share of $2.10. Both exceeded Wall Street expectations.

However, the company's outlook introduced a concern. Apple expects gross margins of 45% to 46% for the December quarter, compared with 47.9% in the reported quarter. Rising memory costs are among the pressures on profitability.

Investors appear to be looking beyond strong iPhone sales and asking how much of that growth will translate into future profits.

Palantir (PLTR): -2.99% after hours

Palantir also delivered impressive results. Quarterly revenue increased 96% year over year to approximately $2.31 billion, while the company raised its full-year revenue forecast to roughly $8.53 billion.

Yet its shares initially declined.

Palantir faces particularly demanding expectations because investors are already pricing in substantial growth from artificial intelligence. Reuters also reported a sharp slowdown in growth of U.S. commercial contract value, giving investors another metric to examine alongside the headline revenue beat.

The lesson from both companies is familiar but important: a company can report excellent financial results while its stock delivers a disappointing reaction.

These percentage moves reflect November 2 extended-hours trading, not completed November 3 regular-session returns.

The declines matter, but neither was an unusually large earnings shock

There is an important distinction between the direction of an earnings reaction and its size.

Ahead of the reports, options pricing suggested approximate expected moves of:

  • Apple: ±4.25%

  • Palantir: ±13.32%

Both initial declines remained inside those ranges.

An options-implied move is an estimate of the magnitude of a possible price change, not a prediction of direction or a guaranteed boundary.

Apple's decline was relatively closer to its expected move. Palantir's was considerably smaller relative to what options traders had priced in.

That distinction prevents us from mistaking every negative earnings reaction for an unusually severe disappointment.

Earnings Mood Score: 4/10, cautious but not panicking

To make sense of the broader environment, we can look beyond individual earnings headlines and use a simplified Earnings Mood Score, ranging from zero to ten.

Current reading: 4/10

Status: Cautious / defensive

Trend: Slightly worsening

This is a simplified assessment of recent earnings reactions, not a forecast for the S&P 500 or a buy-or-sell signal.

Three indicators help explain the reading.

Breadth: 4/10

Recent completed earnings sessions have shown mixed participation. There are companies receiving positive reactions, but weakness has remained significant enough to keep the overall picture cautious.

Big Names: 3/10

Large, widely followed stocks have been a particular source of concern. Recent reactions involving Alphabet, Intel, Apple and Palantir illustrate the pressure in influential technology and growth names.

Surprise Balance: 4/10

Some downside reactions have proved more consequential than upside surprises. This matters because investors are not merely judging whether companies beat estimates, but also whether their share prices respond positively and sustain those gains.

The broader message is that the earnings environment remains cautious and selective rather than uniformly bearish.

Why a few big stocks can change the earnings picture

Consider two different ways of looking at earnings reactions.

One gives each reporting company equal importance. The other gives larger companies more influence according to their market capitalization.

These approaches can produce very different impressions of the same earnings season.

A broad group of smaller companies might rise after reporting, yet a handful of extremely large companies could still pull the capitalization-weighted result into negative territory.

Apple is particularly relevant here because of its enormous market value.

The completed earnings-session review through November 2 shows repeated negative or nearly flat capitalization-weighted outcomes, despite occasional improvements in participation.

This is similar to the distinction between the performance of an equal-weighted stock index and a capitalization-weighted one, although the earnings-reaction sample is not itself an index return.

For investors holding S&P 500 or Nasdaq-linked funds, understanding that concentration is particularly useful.

An earlier investingLive analysis of Alphabet's post-earnings decline explored how large-company earnings disappointments can have consequences well beyond individual shareholders.

What would improve Wall Street's earnings mood?

A reading of 4/10 is not a reason to assume stocks must decline.

It is a reason to pay closer attention to confirmation.

Signs of improvement

More large-cap companies receiving positive earnings reactions would help. So would stronger participation across smaller reporters, fewer outsized downside surprises and evidence that post-earnings gains are holding.

One useful near-term test is whether Apple and Palantir recover their initial losses during the November 3 regular session.

Signs of further deterioration

Additional large-cap selloffs, failed post-earnings rebounds and weakness spreading beyond technology would strengthen the defensive interpretation.

An increase in downside reactions exceeding options-implied expectations would be another important warning.

Importantly, the score would need to be reassessed as new earnings reactions become completed observations.

The most useful earnings lesson may be what happens after the announcement

Strong financial results and positive stock performance are not the same thing.

A headline earnings beat measures reported numbers against published estimates. The share-price reaction also reflects expectations, forward guidance, valuation, positioning and the broader market environment.

Traders can therefore learn something by examining the initial reaction, comparing its size with what options implied, and then watching whether buyers or sellers defend that move during regular trading.

Investors with longer horizons should also distinguish a disappointing short-term reaction from a meaningful deterioration in the company's business outlook.

For a deeper explanation, see our guide to three important stock earnings lessons for investors and traders.

For now, the Earnings Mood Score remains at 4/10: cautious, defensive and slightly worsening, but far from a universal earnings selloff.

The question for the next reporting sessions is whether major companies can start lifting the mood, rather than merely avoiding disappointment.

item.title: More: RBA lifts cash rate to 4.85% in split 6-3 vote, sees inflation above 3% until late 2027
item.description:
For the Australian dollar, the hike delivers little that was not already priced. Markets had assigned an 85% chance to the move, and around one and a half increases by mid-2027 were priced before the meeting. The three-member dissent and the absence of an explicit tightening bias argue against a sustained AUD rally, and leave room for a modest fade if Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference leans cautious. The front end of the curve is likely to stay supported by the higher inflation forecasts, keeping a further hike in play but not locked in. In equities, the RBA’s own assessment that higher rates and the housing downturn are weighing on banks, consumer discretionary and real estate stocks points to continued pressure on those sectors. Energy names remain supported by oil prices the bank assumes will stay well above pre-conflict levels.

-

The RBA hiked again as its inflation forecasts jumped, but a three-member dissent and a non-committal outlook suggest the board is closer to the top of the cycle than its forecasts alone imply.

Summary:

  • The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85%, its fifth increase this year and the highest since 2008; six members voted for the hike and three to hold
  • Headline inflation is forecast to peak at 4.5% in the December quarter, with headline and trimmed mean inflation above 3% until late 2027, about three quarters longer than forecast in August
  • The upgrade reflects higher fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict and a judgement that domestic capacity pressures are tighter than thought; the RBA raised its estimate of the NAIRU to around 4.75%
  • Unemployment averaged 4.6% in the September quarter and is forecast to reach 5.1% by end-2028, while house prices are almost 5% below their March peak
  • The forecasts assume the cash rate rises by around 35 basis points by mid-2027 based on market pricing, up to 50 basis points higher than assumed in August
  • The board said it will be attentive to the data and stopped short of signalling further hikes

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth increase this year and the highest level since 2008. A three-member dissent, however, signalled growing division over how much further policy needs to tighten.

Six members of the Monetary Policy Board voted for the hike, while three preferred to keep the rate at 4.60%. In its statement, the board said inflation remains elevated and broadly based, and that there is an increasing risk higher inflation expectations will become embedded. It judged that further tightening in financial conditions was warranted to support the return of inflation to target.

The accompanying Statement on Monetary Policy showed a material upgrade to the inflation outlook. Headline inflation is now forecast to peak at 4.5% in the December quarter, and both headline and trimmed mean inflation are expected to stay above 3% until late 2027, about three quarters longer than forecast in August. Inflation is not expected to return to the 2.5% midpoint of the target band until mid-2028. Headline inflation was 3.9% over the year to the September quarter, with trimmed mean at 3.7%.

The RBA attributed the revision to two factors. Fuel and other commodity prices have risen sharply since the Middle East conflict re-escalated, with Brent crude around US$115 a barrel at the time of the forecasts. Staff also now judge domestic capacity pressures to be tighter than previously thought, and lifted their estimate of the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation to around 4.75%. The bank also noted that AI-related demand is pushing up prices for technology goods, and that some measures of inflation expectations have risen.

The economy is slowing under the weight of higher rates. House prices were almost 5% below their March peak in September, unemployment averaged 4.6% in the September quarter, and the jobless rate is forecast to rise to 5.1% by end-2028. Strong investment in data centres is partly offsetting weaker household spending and housing activity.

The forecasts assume the cash rate rises by around 35 basis points by mid-2027 in line with market pricing, a path up to 50 basis points higher than in August. On guidance, though, the board said only that it will be attentive to the data and will do what is necessary to bring inflation back to target. That stops short of an explicit commitment to further hikes.

The outcome matched expectations from HSBC and AMP, while the split vote and cautious guidance sit closer to AMP’s hike-and-hold view than to ANZ’s warning of a move to 5.10%.

item.title: After the Binance hack, the simple security rule regulators keep coming back to, hot vs. cold wallets
item.description:
South Korea's financial regulator wants local crypto exchanges to keep more customer assets in cold wallets, offline storage that hackers cannot reach over the internet. The push follows last week's $6.3 billion theft from Binance, which came entirely from the exchange's internet-connected hot wallets. 

  • Following the money: the playbook behind the $6.3bn Binance heist and a suspected $106 million theft

The Financial Services Commission held an emergency meeting with major exchanges on 2 November. It reviewed how exchanges control access to their systems and approve withdrawals, and urged them to raise the share of assets held offline. It did not set a new legal ratio.

The principle behind the request is simple: a hacker can only steal what is reachable online. Understanding the difference between hot and cold wallets explains why that matters, and why it is not a complete answer.

What hot and cold wallets are

A crypto wallet does not hold coins the way a purse holds cash. The coins live on the blockchain. What the wallet holds is the private key, a secret code that authorises spending. Whoever controls the key controls the coins.

The difference between hot and cold is where that key sits.

  • Hot wallet: the key is on a device or system connected to the internet. That makes it fast and convenient. An exchange can process thousands of withdrawals a day automatically, and an individual can trade or pay from a phone app in seconds.
  • Cold wallet: the key is kept offline, on a hardware device, an air-gapped computer that never connects to a network, or even paper. Moving funds takes deliberate, often manual, steps.

A useful comparison is a shop's till versus its bank vault. The till holds enough cash to run the day. The vault holds the rest, and opening it takes time, people and procedures.

Why cold storage offers more protection

Most large crypto thefts are remote. An attacker breaks into a network, often through a single compromised laptop or account, then works their way towards the systems that sign transactions. If the key or the signing system is online, it can be reached that way. If it is offline, there is no network path to it. The attacker would need physical access, or would need to fool the people who operate it.

Cold storage also slows things down, and slowness is a security feature. Moving funds out of cold storage typically requires several people, separate devices and a series of approvals. That gives time for something odd to be noticed. A hot wallet, by design, moves money in seconds, and so does a thief who controls it.

The practical effect is to cap the damage. An exchange with 98% of customer assets in cold storage has only about 2% exposed online at any moment. A breach can still be serious, but it cannot empty the whole platform.

The limits: cold storage is safer, not invulnerable. Keys can be lost, damaged or stolen physically, and staff can be tricked into approving a malicious transfer. And no exchange can run entirely cold, because it needs hot wallets to pay out customer withdrawals. Cold storage reduces how much is at risk. It does not remove the risk.

How the Binance hack fits

Binance is a textbook case of both the strength and the limit of cold storage.

On 29 October, an attacker moved about $6.36 billion out of Binance hot wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs. TRM's assessment is that the attacker gained control of the system Binance uses to sign hot wallet transactions, rather than stealing the keys themselves. Binance's initial investigation reportedly pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng has said the vast majority of user assets sit in cold wallets and only move to hot wallets when customers withdraw. In other words, the vault held. The till was emptied.

The catch is scale. For an exchange of Binance's size, even a small hot wallet share can amount to billions of dollars. Binance says users did not lose money, as it is covering the losses from company funds, but the episode shows that a hot wallet is only as safe as the systems and people that control it.

South Korea's rules and how its exchanges compare

South Korea is one of the few markets that puts a number on cold storage. Under its Virtual Asset User Protection Act, exchanges must keep at least 80% of customer crypto in cold wallets.

Most of the big local platforms already go well beyond that. Cold wallet ratios at the end of September, based on Financial Supervisory Service data cited by local media:

  • Upbit: 99.17%
  • Bithumb: 94.76%
  • Coinone: 85%
  • Digital X (formerly Korbit): 82.79%
  • GOPAX: 80.54%

The spread matters. At 99%, about one coin in a hundred is exposed online. At 80%, it is one in five. That is why the FSC asked exchanges to raise their ratios rather than simply meet the minimum.

The regulator also asked for tighter controls on withdrawal approvals and administrator access, continuous monitoring of deposits and withdrawals, more incident response staff, faster sharing of suspicious access attempts and additional reserves. That list is telling. It targets the approval and signing systems that, on TRM's assessment, were the weak point at Binance. South Korea has its own history here: Upbit lost about $30 million in a hot wallet hack in November 2025 and later moved 99% of assets offline.

What it means for traders and investors

If you hold crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that exchange's balance between hot and cold storage, and on its ability to cover losses if something goes wrong. Two questions are worth asking: how much of customer assets does it keep offline, and what reserves, insurance or company funds stand behind them? Some exchanges publish proof of reserves or cold storage figures; many do not.

The same trade-off applies to individuals. Keeping crypto in an exchange account or phone app is the hot option: convenient for trading, but exposed to that platform's security and your own device. A hardware wallet is the cold option: harder for a remote attacker to reach, but you become responsible for the key, and losing it can mean losing the coins for good.

There is no single right answer. Many holders split the difference, keeping trading funds on an exchange and longer-term holdings offline. The point is to make that choice knowingly rather than by default.

What to watch next

  • Whether South Korea turns the request into a rule. A higher legal minimum than 80%, or new requirements for signing systems and reserves, would mark a real policy shift. For now it is guidance.
  • Binance's root cause report. The exchange has not yet published a full account of how its signing systems were compromised. That will show whether the lesson is about cold storage ratios, or about how hot wallets are controlled.
  • Other regulators. If authorities elsewhere follow with cold storage or disclosure requirements, exchanges may need to publish their ratios, giving users a clearer way to compare platforms.
  • Customer behaviour. Binance saw billions in net outflows when withdrawals reopened. A sustained shift of coins off exchanges and into self-custody would show users are acting on the risk.

What could change the picture: if the Binance investigation finds the breach would have reached cold systems too, the debate moves from how much is stored offline to how approvals are protected. Either way, the useful question for readers is the same: how much of my crypto is reachable online, and who stands behind it if it goes? 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq’s worst month since March 2025 puts returns on AI spending in focus, says BlackRock
item.description:

BlackRock’s emphasis on credit markets as a gauge of how much more AI investment can be financed puts spreads on hyperscaler and AI-linked debt in focus as a leading indicator for tech equities. The pairing of a Treasury rally with the tech selloff also suggests bonds can still cushion portfolios when AI sentiment sours. In emerging markets, the preference for AI supply bottlenecks points toward Asian chipmakers. Friday’s US jobs report is the near-term macro test: stronger wage growth would feed core services inflation and complicate the rally in Treasuries.

---

---

BlackRock still believes in AI, but says the spending bill is now big enough that investors are demanding proof of returns, and the rest of the market is quietly out-earning the tech giants.

Summary:

  • BlackRock says investor scrutiny of AI is intensifying this earnings season, after the Nasdaq posted its worst month since March 2025
  • Earnings growth for the S&P 500 excluding the “magnificent seven” is running at about 29%, ahead of roughly 18% for the megacaps, the first such flip since 2022
  • Hyperscaler capex has risen to about $650 billion over the past year from about $360 billion, while incremental margins have fallen to about 28% from 40%
  • The firm recently downgraded US equities to neutral to lock in profits but says its conviction in AI remains intact, and it is overweight emerging market equities via AI bottlenecks
  • It sees credit markets as a key signpost as the AI buildout becomes more debt-financed; 10-year Treasury yields fell nearly 6 basis points to 4.93% last week
  • BlackRock is watching October US jobs data for wage pressure that could lift core services inflation

BlackRock says investors are demanding clearer evidence that the AI spending boom can deliver returns. Earnings leadership in the US stock market has also shifted away from the largest technology companies for the first time in four years.

In its weekly commentary, the BlackRock Investment Institute said scrutiny of AI is intensifying this earnings season, after the Nasdaq Composite posted its worst month since March 2025. Four years of heavy AI investment have pushed earnings expectations sharply higher, and rising capital spending is squeezing free cash flow, in some cases pushing it negative.

The backdrop for megacap tech has changed quickly. According to BlackRock, earnings growth for the rest of the S&P 500 is running at about 29% in the third quarter, compared with roughly 18% for the “magnificent seven” stocks, with figures including estimates. That is the first time the smaller group has outpaced the megacaps since 2022. Consensus expects overall S&P 500 earnings growth of about 30%, a third straight quarter above 20%, based on LSEG data.

BlackRock highlighted a growing tension between strong AI demand and the cost of meeting it. Hyperscaler capital spending has climbed to about $650 billion over the past year from about $360 billion in the prior year, according to Bloomberg data. Operating margins have edged up to 27.1% from 26.9%, but incremental margins, the extra profit generated by each additional dollar of revenue, have fallen to about 28% from 40%. That raises the question of whether returns can keep pace with investment, the firm said.

There are encouraging signs. BlackRock’s analysis finds companies outside the tech and communication sectors with higher AI adoption are on track for 3% faster earnings growth this quarter than lower adopters. Cloud growth at Microsoft and Alphabet also points to sustained demand.

As the buildout relies more on debt, the firm said credit markets have become an important signal of how much further AI investment can be financed, and at what cost. US Treasuries rallied alongside last week’s tech selloff, with 10-year yields falling nearly 6 basis points to 4.93% after the Federal Reserve held rates.

BlackRock downgraded US equities to neutral last month to lock in profits but said its conviction in AI fundamentals remains intact. It prefers companies and listed infrastructure positioned to benefit from bottlenecks in the buildout, which underpins its overweight in emerging market equities, particularly in Asia. Attention now turns to Friday’s October jobs report, where BlackRock expects signs of stronger wage pressure that could add to core services inflation. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Blackstone’s Gray sees more AI equity fundraising ahead from major tech firms
item.description:
Gray’s comments reinforce a theme running through this week’s news flow: the AI buildout is increasingly being financed by issuing shares, not just from cash flow and debt. For equity markets, more issuance from major tech companies means a heavier supply of new stock and potential dilution for existing holders. That can weigh on prices around deals, as Oracle’s discounted $10 billion sale shows. Coming from the head of one of the largest investors in data centers, the remarks also signal confidence that AI demand is durable enough to justify the capital. That is supportive for infrastructure, power and chip suppliers, even if the funding burden falls on the spenders. The key question for investors is whether new equity is priced at a premium or a discount, which will show how willing markets are to keep financing the buildout.

-

The AI spending race is outgrowing what cash flow and borrowing can cover, and Blackstone’s Jon Gray expects the biggest tech companies to come back to equity investors for more.

Summary:

  • Blackstone President Jon Gray said more global equity fundraising will be needed to keep pace with the enormous demand from AI industry growth. Info via Reuters. 
  • He said most major technology companies are expected to raise more capital
  • Gray spoke at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit on Tuesday
  • Blackstone is the world’s largest alternative asset manager, with nearly $1.4 trillion in assets under management, and has been investing heavily in AI-related infrastructure
  • His comments come as Oracle prepares a $10 billion share sale and other large tech firms turn to equity markets to fund AI spending

Blackstone President Jon Gray said on Tuesday that more global equity fundraising will be needed to keep up with the enormous demand created by the growth of the artificial intelligence industry. He added that most major technology companies are expected to raise more capital. 

Gray made the remarks at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, Reuters reported. His comments point to an AI buildout whose funding needs are outgrowing what the largest companies can cover from operating cash flow and borrowing alone.

Blackstone is the world’s largest alternative asset manager, meaning it invests in assets beyond publicly traded stocks and bonds. It oversees nearly $1.4 trillion across real estate, private equity, credit, infrastructure, life sciences, growth equity, secondaries and hedge funds. Its investors include pension funds, insurance companies and individuals. The firm, led by Chairman and Chief Executive Stephen Schwarzman, has positioned itself as a major investor in the physical infrastructure behind AI, including data centers and energy. Its recent activity includes a joint venture to develop a data center campus in Michigan. Gray, as president, is the firm’s second-ranking executive.

That gives Gray’s view particular weight, since Blackstone sits on the supply side of the buildout and sees demand for capacity firsthand.

His comments match a pattern seen this week. Oracle is preparing to price a $10 billion share sale, alongside a matching bond offering, to fund its AI expansion, and is reportedly offering a discount of around 11% to attract buyers. Pershing Square noted in its latest shareholder letter that Meta had announced a $98 billion equity raise. Anthropic is also preparing for a public listing.

The shift toward equity funding cuts both ways for investors. It allows companies to keep investing without overloading their balance sheets, but it dilutes existing shareholders and adds a steady supply of new stock to the market. How readily investors absorb that supply, and at what price, is becoming a key measure of confidence in the AI spending cycle.

item.title: JPMorgan’s four midterm scenarios: S&P 500 seen moving between -0.25% and +1.25%

For tech, the desk plays down the risk of AI regulation under a Democratic Congress, given the presidential veto, but flags potential selling within the AI theme. For oil, a Republican sweep is seen as potentially giving Trump more room to press on with the Iran campaign, linking the vote directly to the crude risk premium.

JPMorgan’s trading desk expects only modest moves in US stocks whatever the midterm result, with the most likely outcome producing the smallest reaction and the least likely the biggest gain.

  • JPMorgan’s trading desk mapped four midterm outcomes, using Bloomberg prediction market odds as of November 1
  • Democratic House and Senate (66%): the S&P 500 is seen moving between -0.25% and +0.5%, with slightly lower long-end yields on reduced deficit spending
  • Democratic House, Republican Senate (26%): stocks seen rising 0.5% to 1%, with Democrats expected to rein in deficit spending through control of government finances
  • Republican House and Senate (7%): stocks seen climbing 1% to 1.25%, with long-end yields higher on continued elevated deficit spending
  • Republican House, Democratic Senate (1%): stocks seen rising 0.25% to 0.75%, with budget fights and possible shutdowns

JPMorgan’s trading desk expects US stocks to move only modestly in response to Tuesday’s midterm elections. It sees the most likely outcome producing the smallest reaction and the least likely outcome the biggest gain.

In a scenario map based on Bloomberg prediction market odds as of November 1, the bank’s market intelligence team assigned a 66% probability to Democrats winning both the House and the Senate. In that case, it sees the S&P 500 moving between a 0.25% decline and a 0.5% gain, with long-end Treasury yields edging lower on reduced deficit spending.

The desk said investors may fear a sell-off in AI stocks on concerns over regulation under a Democratic Congress, but argued Trump would not sign legislation limiting AI and Democrats would lack a veto-proof majority. It described any dip as a potential buying opportunity for AI bulls, while flagging the risk that investors cut exposure within the AI theme. It also noted possible congressional investigations involving Trump-linked donors, including large technology companies.

A split Congress, with Democrats taking the House and Republicans holding the Senate, was given 26% odds. JPMorgan sees stocks rising 0.5% to 1% in that scenario, with Democratic control of government finances expected to reduce deficit spending and possibly lower long-end yields. It said the arrangement would effectively remove impeachment risk, while gridlock would bring budget fights in 2027 that have historically had limited economic impact.

A Republican sweep, at 7% odds, would deliver the strongest gain, with the S&P 500 seen climbing 1% to 1.25%. The desk said the status quo would bring no new regulatory risks but would keep deficit spending elevated, pushing long-end yields higher. It added that such an outcome could encourage Trump to continue the Iran campaign until a deal favorable to the US or an Iranian capitulation.

The least likely result, a Republican House and Democratic Senate at 1%, is seen lifting stocks 0.25% to 0.75%, with budget fights and possible shutdowns.

The modest ranges suggest markets have largely priced in the expected outcome, leaving a surprise result as the bigger potential catalyst.

The result is a two-way market: crude is exposed to a sharp rebound if a broader operation materialises, while continued restraint and progress through mediators would support Monday’s lower levels. Iran’s threat to retaliate within and beyond the Middle East keeps tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz as the central risk.

--

Washington is quietly hitting Iranian targets while Trump talks down the prospect of war, leaving oil traders to weigh public reassurance against preparations for a possible post-election operation.

Summary:

  • The US struck Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, US officials said, confirming earlier unverified reports of explosions there
  • The attack is the latest in a series of limited strikes the US has carried out against Iran in recent weeks without public announcement
  • Some officials described the strikes as defensive, aimed at limiting Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz
  • Trump said on Monday the US had not been fighting Iran for months and answered “no” when asked about strikes after the midterms, though officials said he is weighing all options
  • The US has told Gulf nations to prepare for a short and intense operation shortly after the election, according to the report
  • Iran said the onus is on Washington to reach a deal, while Iranian leaders have warned of retaliation inside and beyond the Middle East if the conflict reignites

The United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, US officials said, confirming earlier unverified reports of explosions there. The strike was the latest in a string of limited attacks Washington has quietly carried out against Iran in recent weeks, even as President Donald Trump played down the risk of renewed war, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported.

The strike came on the same day Trump told reporters the conflict with Iran had effectively ended, saying “we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.” Officials told the Journal, however, that smaller-scale strikes had been under way for several weeks. Some described them as defensive, intended to deny Iran the freedom to attack commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Unlike earlier phases of the war, the attacks have not been publicly announced. One official said the campaign was being kept quiet to avoid signalling any intention to resume major combat.

Qeshm sits at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz and hosts a large underground missile site, a naval base and a major desalination plant. The US has targeted the island in earlier rounds of fighting, and officials have discussed seizing it, according to the Journal. The Defense Department referred questions to US Central Command, which did not immediately comment.

The report also pointed to preparations for a possible wider campaign. Centcom has moved additional missile defenses and munitions into the region, and the US has told Gulf nations to prepare for a short, intense operation shortly after Tuesday’s midterm elections, the Journal said. Trump has said for weeks that all-out war could resume after the vote. Senior officials have presented options ranging from further airstrikes to tighter sanctions and a stricter blockade on Iranian trade.

In the hours before voting, though, Trump softened his tone. He said “no” when asked whether he was considering strikes after the midterms, and he and Vice President JD Vance suggested negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program could still succeed. Administration officials said the president continues to weigh all his options.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said responsibility for any deal now lies with Washington and described Iran’s demands as reasonable. Senior Iranian figures, including Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, have warned that Iran would retaliate both within and beyond the region if the US reignites the conflict.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Following the money: the playbook behind the $6.3bn Binance heist and a suspected $106 million theft
item.description:
Two crypto thefts in less than a week show the same playbook. Stolen crypto moves along a predictable path, and the path is shaped by one fear above all others: being frozen. Knowing that path helps explain how much stolen money can be recovered, how much cannot, and why some of it may eventually reach the market.

The big one is Binance. On 29 October, an attacker moved about $6.36 billion out of the exchange's hot wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs. A hot wallet is an internet-connected wallet an exchange uses to process withdrawals. The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, and it is the largest crypto theft on record.

The smaller case is unconfirmed. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT said on Monday that an unnamed entity in the European Union may have lost more than $106 million from accounts at several exchanges on Sunday. Neither the victim nor the exchanges have been named, so treat it as a suspected theft. It is still useful, because the funds appear to have taken the same route.

Step 1: Get out of stablecoins, fast

Stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC are the thief's biggest problem. Their issuers can freeze tokens sitting in a specific wallet, which turns stolen dollars into dead weight.

That is exactly what happened at Binance. TRM Labs says Tether froze about 971 million USDT in the attacker's main receiving wallet 37 minutes after the main sweep, and Circle froze 823 million USDC minutes later. Counting freezes by Tether, Circle, Ripple, World Liberty Financial and Arbitrum's Security Council, TRM puts the total at roughly $2.7 billion. Binance has given a figure of about $3 billion.

The attacker raced those freezes and paid heavily to do it. TRM says about 325 million USDT was sold to market makers for roughly 122,300 ETH, implying a discount of more than 10% to the market price. Another 60 million USDT was posted as collateral on lending protocol Aave to borrow about 19,760 ETH. Accepting a large haircut tells you how much the thief valued escaping a freeze.

The suspected EU theft started the same way. ZachXBT said the funds were withdrawn in USDC and USDT and the USDC was swapped for Ether.

Step 2: Split the trail and hop chains

Once the money is in assets no issuer can freeze, mainly ETH and BTC, the goal shifts to making it hard to follow.

One method is the peel chain. TRM says the 18,270 BTC taken from Binance was split into round pieces of 1,000 and 100 BTC within the same block, creating many smaller trails instead of one large one. Investigators also reported automated activity, with funds sent back and forth among wallets, including addresses used earlier, to confuse tracing.

Another method is chain hopping. Cross-chain bridges move assets from one blockchain to another, which forces investigators to pick up the trail on a different network. In the second, smaller case flagged on Monday, on-chain monitor Onchain Lens said funds from a wallet linked to King, a Solana arbitrage bot, moved through several Solana wallets and then to Ethereum using the bridging service Mayan. King's operator has not confirmed a compromise, but the pattern is a textbook example.

TRM notes the early Binance laundering leaned on market makers and lending protocols rather than the bridge-heavy route used after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. It expects bridges, swap services and over-the-counter brokers to feature in the next stage.

Step 3: Go dark, then cash out

The final stretch is about breaking the public trail altogether and turning crypto into usable money.

The suspected EU theft shows the go-dark step clearly. ZachXBT said the funds passed through instant exchange services, including WellWallet and Kyrrex, and were converted into Monero through a swap service called Wagyu. Instant exchanges let users swap one coin for another quickly, often with lighter checks than a major exchange. Monero is a privacy coin: unlike Bitcoin or Ethereum, where every transfer sits on a public ledger, it hides senders, receivers and amounts by default. Once funds are in Monero, on-chain tracing becomes far harder.

The last step is converting to cash, usually through over-the-counter brokers and professional laundering networks. Experts quoted by CNBC said these networks reduce the chances of recovery. This stage can stretch over weeks or months, which is why stolen funds can keep moving long after the headlines fade.

Why it matters for traders and investors

The path explains the split between what was frozen and what was not. Stablecoins were the recoverable part. ETH and BTC were not. TRM says the Binance attacker still controls more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about $2.4 billion, beyond any issuer's reach.

That creates a possible overhang. If large amounts of that ETH or BTC are eventually sold, it would add supply to the market. The timing and route are unknown, and laundering often happens in smaller pieces over a long period, so it should not be treated as an imminent sell-off. It is a factor to monitor, not a forecast.

There is also a demand side. Binance co-CEO Yi He has said the exchange set aside more than $6.34 billion of company funds to replace the stolen assets, and reports say part of that will be bought through over-the-counter deals and exchange trading.

For individual holders, the lesson is about where risk sits. This theft hit Binance's own hot wallets, and Binance says it is covering the losses, so customers have not been told they lost money. But it is a reminder that crypto held on any exchange depends on that exchange's security. Stablecoin freezes cut both ways too: they helped here, but they also show that issuers can control tokens in any wallet.

What to watch next

  • Movement from the attacker's ETH and BTC wallets. TRM is monitoring the peel chain and consolidation wallets. Large transfers to exchanges or OTC desks would be the first sign stolen funds are heading for sale.
  • Binance's root cause. The exchange has not yet published a full explanation of how its signing systems were compromised. That matters for judging whether other platforms face the same risk.
  • Confirmation of the EU case. If the victim or exchanges are named, or a confirmed loss figure emerges, the $106 million theft becomes a story in its own right. Until then it stays a suspected theft.
  • Updated freeze totals. Any change in how much has been frozen, or returned, shifts the estimate of what remains in the attacker's hands.

What could change the picture: if the stolen ETH and BTC sit untouched for months, the overhang matters less in the near term. If large amounts start reaching exchanges, it becomes a more direct supply question. Either way, watching the wallets is more useful than guessing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD
item.description:
The move signals that Beijing is uncomfortable with the pace of the yuan’s recent strength. That gives USD/CNY and USD/CNH a floor near current levels rather than reversing the trend outright. Its direct liquidity effect is modest, so traders are likely to treat it as a warning shot, with the daily fixing the main tool to watch for follow-through. The signal reaches beyond China: a PBOC leaning against appreciation tends to temper gains in other Asian currencies that trade alongside the yuan, such as the Korean won and Taiwan dollar. It can also weigh at the margin on the Australian dollar, which often trades as a China proxy. The timing matters too, with the US dollar already softer on Iran diplomacy hopes. If the dollar weakens further, the PBOC may need stronger signals to hold the line.

---

---

China’s central bank is making dollars scarcer onshore to take some heat out of a strengthening yuan, a modest move in size but a clear signal of where Beijing wants the currency to go.

Summary:

  • The People’s Bank of China will raise the foreign exchange deposit reserve ratio for financial institutions to 6% from 4%, effective November 15
  • The PBOC said the move is intended to strengthen the management of foreign exchange liquidity at financial institutions
  • The ratio sets how much of their foreign currency deposits banks must hold in reserve; raising it reduces the dollars available onshore
  • The PBOC has typically raised the ratio to slow yuan appreciation and cut it to support the currency when it weakens
  • Monday’s USD/CNY fixing of around 6.71 was notably weaker than the roughly 6.66 Reuters estimate, another sign the PBOC is leaning against yuan strength
  • The direct liquidity impact is modest, so the policy signal is likely to matter more to markets than the mechanics

China’s central bank will require banks to hold a larger share of their foreign currency deposits in reserve. The move is a technical tightening of onshore dollar liquidity that markets are likely to read as a signal that Beijing wants to slow the yuan’s rise.

The People’s Bank of China said it will raise the foreign exchange deposit reserve ratio for financial institutions by 2 percentage points, to 6% from 4%, from November 15. It described the step as a way to strengthen the management of foreign exchange liquidity in the banking system.

The ratio works much like the better-known reserve requirement on yuan deposits, but it applies to deposits held in foreign currencies, mostly US dollars. When the ratio rises, banks must park more of those dollars with the central bank, leaving fewer available to lend, invest or sell in the onshore market. With dollars harder to come by, they become relatively more expensive against the yuan, which takes some pressure off the Chinese currency’s appreciation.

The PBOC uses the tool in both directions. It raised the ratio twice in 2021, when the yuan was climbing strongly, and cut it in 2022 and again in 2023 as the currency weakened and the central bank sought to support it. The ratio had stood at 4% since the last cut, making this the first increase in several years.

The size of the move is modest. When the PBOC cut the ratio by the same 2 percentage points in 2022, ANZ estimated it would add around $20 billion of foreign currency to the market, which is small relative to China’s currency market. The signal, rather than the cash amount, is the main point.

Other indicators point the same way. On Monday, the PBOC set its daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 6.71, considerably weaker for the yuan than the roughly 6.66 that Reuters’ survey of models had expected. That suggests the central bank was already leaning against the currency’s strength. The PBOC has also said it aims to keep the yuan broadly stable and to guard against the risk of the exchange rate overshooting.

For traders, the practical takeaway is that Beijing is signalling a preference for slower, steadier yuan gains. It is not reversing the currency’s direction. The daily fixing will be the clearest guide to whether more steps follow, particularly if the US dollar weakens further. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran talks stall as reported US strike and CIA advice undercut oil’s 4% deal-hope drop
item.description:
Monday’s near 4% drop in crude priced in a diplomatic opening that the subsequent news flow does little to support. That leaves room for some of the decline to retrace if the standoff persists. The terms on the table show how large the stakes are for supply: Iran’s plan links reopening the Strait of Hormuz and a US waiver on Iranian oil sales to an end of the US blockade of its ports, so a deal would release a significant flow of barrels. That makes the market asymmetric. Genuine progress could push prices sharply lower, but stalled talks, reported US strikes and advice in Washington to keep up economic pressure argue for a geopolitical risk premium staying in place. Any confirmation of US military action, or a firm Iranian response, is the next catalyst for crude.

---

Oil sold off on hopes of an Iran deal, but stalled talks, a reported US strike and Washington’s preference for sustained pressure suggest that optimism was premature.

Summary:

  • Days of Iranian talks with Qatari mediators ended on Monday with altered proposals but no breakthrough; Tehran said contacts with the US continue through mediators
  • Iran said its seven-step plan, rejected by President Trump in September, remains the basis for talks and has been condensed so it could be implemented within two days
  • The plan calls for the US to end its blockade of Iranian ports and waive sanctions on oil sales, with Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz; Iran rejects handing its highly enriched uranium to a third country
  • Oil fell nearly 4% on Monday on deal hopes, though Iranian sources said a new US attack was still seen as more likely than an agreement
  • Later reports of explosions on Qeshm Island, an Israeli media report of a US strike there, and an IRGC claim of downing a US drone remain unconfirmed
  • CIA Director John Ratcliffe is reportedly advising Trump to maintain a “no war, no deal” approach and let economic pressure continue

Iran said on Monday that contacts with the United States to end their eight-month war were continuing through mediators, after days of talks with Qatari officials ended without a breakthrough. A series of developments since then has undercut the optimism that sent oil prices sharply lower.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said messages were being exchanged through mediators but described the issue as complex, Reuters reported. Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said consultations had been intensive and that the outcome depended on Washington. Baghaei said Iran’s seven-step plan, which Trump rejected in September, remained the basis for discussions. It has been condensed so that it could be implemented within two days, he said, though Iran’s core position that nuclear talks can only resume once its conditions are met has not changed.

The plan would require the US to lift its blockade on Iranian ports, grant a waiver on Iranian oil sales and cancel new sanctions, with Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and wider issues left for later talks. Iranian officials also ruled out transferring the country’s highly enriched uranium to a third country.

Oil prices fell nearly 4% on Monday on hopes the mediation could produce a diplomatic solution, even as Iranian sources told Reuters they still saw a renewed US attack as more likely than a deal.

Hours later, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported several explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with the cause unclear. Israeli broadcaster N12 reported that a US strike had hit an air defense system there as part of limited, unannounced US operations in recent weeks. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards separately claimed to have shot down a US drone over the strait. None of those reports has been officially confirmed.

Adding to the picture, Axios reported, citing sources, that CIA Director John Ratcliffe is advising Trump to maintain a “no war, no deal” status quo. He reportedly argues that sustained economic pressure will force further Iranian concessions or provoke internal unrest.

Taken together, the developments point to a prolonged standoff rather than an imminent agreement. For energy markets, the key questions are whether Washington engages with Iran’s condensed proposal, and whether the low-level military friction around the Strait of Hormuz escalates further. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oracle set to price $10 billion share sale at reported 11% discount
item.description:
A double-digit discount would signal investors are demanding a sizeable concession to fund Oracle’s AI buildout, adding to pressure on the stock after a sharp slide since last week’s investor day. For the wider AI trade, it reinforces a growing split between cash-rich hyperscalers that can self-fund and companies such as Oracle and the neoclouds that need outside capital. Demand for the parallel $10 billion bond deal, and where it prices relative to Oracle’s existing debt, will be a key gauge of credit market appetite for AI-linked borrowers. Once the deal prices, the removal of supply overhang could steady the shares if the discount proves to be a clearing level rather than a sign of weak demand.

Oracle is paying up to raise equity for its AI buildout, with a reported 11% discount underlining how much harder it is to fund the spending race without a hyperscaler’s balance sheet.

Summary:

  • Oracle is poised to price its $10 billion share sale at an 11% discount, according to reports; it is not yet clear which share price the discount is measured against
  • The stock sale runs alongside a separate $10 billion bond offering in six tranches maturing between 2029 and 2046; neither deal depends on the other
  • The combined $20 billion uses up the full funding cap Oracle set at its investor day last week, split evenly between equity and debt
  • At Friday’s close of about $131, the sale implied about 77 million new shares, roughly 2.5% dilution; a discount means more shares and slightly higher dilution
  • Oracle shares fell about 6% to 7% on Monday, and the company has lost nearly $65 billion in market value since last Wednesday
  • Proceeds are earmarked for general corporate purposes, which can include capital spending and debt repayment

Oracle is poised to price a $10 billion sale of new shares at an 11% discount, according to reports. The move underlines the cost of raising capital for its artificial intelligence buildout. It was not immediately clear whether the discount is measured against Friday’s closing price or Monday’s lower close, which would change the size of the concession and the number of shares issued.

The equity sale is one of two offerings Oracle filed on Monday, alongside a separate $10 billion sale of senior notes across six tranches with maturities from 2029 to 2046. The deals are independent of each other. Oracle said the proceeds would be used for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditure, debt repayment, acquisitions, dividends and share buybacks. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are among the bookrunners on the stock sale.

The timing has unsettled investors. At its investor day last Wednesday, Oracle pledged to limit new capital-market funding for its fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to $20 billion, split evenly between equity and debt, and the shares rallied 12% the next day. Five days later it moved to raise the entire amount.

Based on Friday’s closing price of about $131, the stock sale implied roughly 77 million new shares, lifting the share count to about 3.1 billion and diluting existing holders by around 2.5%. Pricing at a discount would require more shares to raise the same sum. The bond sale would add about 8% to Oracle’s total debt of around $125 billion.

Oracle shares fell about 6% to 7% on Monday, extending a slide that has wiped nearly $65 billion off its market value since Wednesday. The company has reaffirmed fiscal 2027 guidance for at least $90 billion in revenue and $8.10 in adjusted earnings per share.

The deal highlights a widening divide in how the AI buildout is financed. In its latest shareholder letter, Pershing Square argued that the funding needs of Oracle and the neoclouds should not be confused with those of the largest hyperscalers, which it said can largely fund their spending from operating cash flow. Final pricing of both offerings, and demand for the bonds in particular, will show how much investors are willing to commit to Oracle’s side of that divide. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6489 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
